title: Best Thai cities for digital nomads: Chiang Mai, Bangkok, Koh Phangan, Phuket and Hua Hin
summary: Thailand has fast internet, plenty of co-working space and a visa made for remote workers. This guide compares five popular bases on internet, co-working, cost of living and lifestyle, then explains the visa choice (DTV or LTR) and the tax rules you should know before staying more than six months.
seoTitle: Thailand for Digital Nomads: Best Cities, Visas & Tax
seoDescription: Chiang Mai, Bangkok, Koh Phangan, Phuket or Hua Hin? Compare internet, co-working and living costs, choose between the DTV and LTR visa, and understand Thai tax residency.

sections.heading: How to read this guide
paragraphs: Every city here has reliable fibre internet, good mobile data and cafes where laptops are welcome. The differences are in cost, climate, community and how easy it is to get around.

The monthly budgets are rough ranges for one person, covering rent, food, transport, co-working and phone. They are our own estimates, not official figures. Your spending depends on your lifestyle, the season and the exchange rate, so treat them as a starting point.

sections.heading: Chiang Mai
paragraphs: Chiang Mai is Thailand's classic nomad base: a relaxed northern city with the moated Old City, the Nimman area full of cafes, and one of the largest remote-work communities in Asia. It is cheaper than Bangkok and the islands, and easy to reach by domestic flight.
list: Internet: fast home fibre is standard in condos, and 4G/5G coverage is good across the city.
Co-working: many spaces around Nimman, Santitham and the Old City, with day passes and monthly memberships.
Budget: roughly 30,000 to 60,000 THB a month.
Watch out for: the burning season (roughly February to April), when air quality can be very poor. Many nomads leave for those months.

sections.heading: Bangkok
paragraphs: Bangkok suits you if you want big-city energy, the best transport links in the country and a serious business scene. The BTS Skytrain and MRT make life without a car easy, and there is every kind of food, gym and neighbourhood.
list: Internet: the fastest and most reliable in Thailand, with high-speed fibre in almost every condo building.
Co-working: a wide choice from budget spaces to premium serviced offices, especially along Sukhumvit, Silom and Ari.
Budget: roughly 40,000 to 90,000 THB a month, depending on how central you live.
Watch out for: traffic, heat, and seasonal air pollution in the cooler months.

sections.heading: Koh Phangan
paragraphs: Koh Phangan, in the Gulf of Thailand, has grown a strong community of remote workers, yoga teachers and wellness fans away from the Full Moon Party beach. Life is slower, nature is close and the community is tight-knit.
list: Internet: fibre is available in many villas and cafes, but outages during storms happen. Keep a mobile data backup.
Co-working: a handful of dedicated spaces, mostly around Srithanu and Thong Sala.
Budget: roughly 35,000 to 70,000 THB a month; prices rise sharply in high season.
Watch out for: getting there takes a ferry, you will likely need a scooter, and healthcare is limited compared with the mainland.

sections.heading: Phuket
paragraphs: Phuket combines beaches with proper infrastructure: an international airport, private hospitals, international schools and big supermarkets. It suits nomads who want island life without giving up convenience, and it is a Muay Thai hotspot too.
list: Internet: good fibre coverage in most residential areas and condos.
Co-working: spaces around Rawai, Kata, Chalong and Bang Tao, plus plenty of laptop-friendly cafes.
Budget: roughly 45,000 to 100,000 THB a month; one of the most expensive places to live in Thailand.
Watch out for: high-season prices, limited public transport, and roads that are dangerous for inexperienced scooter riders.

sections.heading: Hua Hin
paragraphs: Hua Hin is a calm seaside town a few hours south of Bangkok, popular with Thai families, retirees and remote workers who want a quiet routine. It is easy to pop up to Bangkok by road or train.
list: Internet: reliable fibre in condos and houses.
Co-working: only a few dedicated spaces, but many quiet cafes.
Budget: roughly 30,000 to 60,000 THB a month.
Watch out for: a smaller nomad community and a quieter social life than Chiang Mai or Bangkok.

sections.heading: The visa angle: DTV or LTR?
paragraphs: Short trips of up to 30 days can often be done on the visa exemption, which from 15 September 2026 covers tourism for 54 nationalities. Working online on a tourist entry is a grey area, so if you plan to work while you are here, use a visa designed for it.

The Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) is the main option for most nomads. It is valid for five years with multiple entries, allows up to 180 days per entry plus one extension of up to 180 days, and costs 10,000 THB. You need 500,000 THB (or equivalent) in savings and proof of your remote work, such as an employment contract or client work. It lets you work for foreign employers and clients, but not for Thai companies.

The Long-Term Resident (LTR) visa, run by the Board of Investment, is aimed at higher earners. Its "Work-from-Thailand Professional" category is for employees of established overseas companies, usually with a personal income of at least USD 80,000 a year over the last two years (USD 40,000 with a master's degree or higher). It gives a 10-year visa, fewer reporting duties and, importantly, a tax exemption on foreign income brought into Thailand. The fee is 50,000 THB.

sections.heading: Tax: what changes after 180 days
paragraphs: Your visa does not decide your tax position; the number of days you spend in Thailand does. Under the Revenue Code, if you are in Thailand for 180 days or more in a calendar year, you are a Thai tax resident for that year. Non-residents pay Thai tax only on income from Thai sources.

Thai tax residents pay tax on income from Thai sources and on foreign income they bring into Thailand. Since 1 January 2024, under Revenue Department Instruction Por. 161/2566, foreign income is taxable in the year you bring it into Thailand, whenever it was earned. Instruction Por. 162/2566 exempts foreign income earned before 1 January 2024. As of September 2026 these rules still apply; a proposed exemption for income remitted within a set period has been discussed but is not law.

In practice, living in Thailand for more than half the year and paying your rent from a foreign salary may create a Thai tax bill. A tax treaty between Thailand and your home country may give credit for tax you already paid. Thai personal income tax rates are progressive, up to 35%, and returns are due by the end of March for the previous year.

LTR holders in the Work-from-Thailand Professional category are exempt from Thai tax on foreign income they bring in. DTV holders get no special tax treatment. Tax is personal and complicated, so speak to a qualified tax adviser before you settle in.

faqs.q: Can I work remotely on a DTV?
faqs.a: Yes, for foreign employers or clients. The DTV does not allow you to work for a Thai company or take local jobs; that needs a work permit and a different visa.

faqs.q: Do I pay Thai tax on a DTV?
faqs.a: Possibly. If you spend 180 days or more in Thailand in a calendar year you become a Thai tax resident, and foreign income you bring into Thailand can then be taxed. The DTV gives no tax exemption.
Chiang Mai and Hua Hin are generally the most affordable of the five. Phuket and central Bangkok are usually the most expensive.

faqs.q: Is the LTR worth it for a nomad?
faqs.a: Only if you meet its strict income and employer rules. For high earners who plan to live in Thailand most of the year, the tax exemption on foreign income can make the 50,000 THB fee worthwhile.
